site.name: tinyactors
site.tagline: Like SQLite, but for actors: statecharts that run in your process.

audience.name: Agent-platform engineer
audience.description: A senior backend engineer building a multi-tenant backend for AI agents, chats or realtime sessions, in Node.js or Bun, evaluating a runtime for one long-lived stateful unit per session or tenant.
audience.knows: Actor systems and Cloudflare Durable Objects; Rivet; XState; containers and serverless limits. Little SCXML.
audience.want: Whether it runs inside the backend they already have
Memory per actor and how many fit in one process, with the benchmark behind the number
Hibernation and snapshots for idle sessions
A code example before any concept
audience.task: npm install and run the first chart
Compare it with Rivet and Durable Objects
audience.objection: Another runtime or platform to operate?
Is anyone running this in production?
Will an agent really write good charts?

audience.name: Workflow developer who tests
audience.description: A backend developer, often in Python, whose long-running business logic (retries, timeouts, payments, multi-day waits) is hard to test and has been hand-rolled as state machines or considered for Temporal.
audience.knows: Temporal or Celery and their replay or retry models; pytest; the pain of sleeping in tests and of flaky timing.
audience.want: A simulated clock that runs a week of timeouts in milliseconds
The whole flow written down as states and transitions
Effects as events their code performs, so tests need no mocks of the world
Commands that check, compare and run charts in CI, with no program to write
audience.task: Write one workflow as a chart
audience.objection: Does it need Docker or a cluster like Temporal?
What survives a crash of the process?
Will the simulated run match production?

audience.name: Tech lead who approves dependencies
audience.description: An architect or tech lead deciding whether the team may depend on tinyactors across services, clients and devices (Node.js, Python, the browser, C), and accountable when it fails.
audience.knows: Reasons like sqlite.org's "when to use" page: what it is for, what it is not for. Knows SQLite, embedded libraries, and the cost of a new server.
audience.want: An honest "use it when, do not use it when"
The failure semantics of one process: what is lost, what a snapshot or migration keeps
One chart running the same everywhere
The test suite that backs "passes all"
audience.task: Write the case for the team
audience.objection: One process is one point of failure.
What happens to state when the host dies?
Are we locked in to this runtime or its chart format?

voice.name: Reference
voice.description: The developer voice at its plainest, and the rules every other voice keeps: facts a reader looks up, said once, with the product as the subject.
voice.rule: Headlines, headings and claims' statements are 1 to 8 words, sentence case, with no period at the end ("Build a team chat"); a question keeps its question mark.
A headline states a benefit, a heading its finding, and a sentence before a block what the block shows.
A lede states the page's strongest facts, never a list of what is coming.
Sentences are at most 30 words and vary in length: most under 20, about a third under 8, so a short sentence lands each point.
A paragraph is one to three sentences; reference prose is one or two before each table, list or block, saying what it holds.
Join a cause to its effect in one sentence with "so", "because" or "which is why", rather than two sentences side by side.
A number says what was measured, on what and with what, and which way the setup leans; a measured number replaces any adjective.
No adjective that does not measure something, no hype words, no emoji. Never write "formal verification".
A negative names the reader's current tool or belief ("never opens a socket", "no server to operate"); never deny what nobody assumed.
The reader is "you". No "we" and no contractions in reference.
No rhetorical questions. A question only quotes the reader: an objection, or a heading of frequently asked questions.
Actions are a verb and an object, 2 to 4 words.
Name SCXML and actor terms exactly (state, event, transition, actor, host). The product name is lowercase: tinyactors.
No serial comma: "states, events and transitions".
Examples are things people build: an order, a payment, a subscription, a chat session; never a door, a light switch or a traffic light.
Never add a claim, number, name or capability that the page or its sources do not state.
Never name the reader's role ("as a tech lead", "for operators"); write for them by choosing what to explain.
Never explain how the site is made (that a page is generated, captured or checked); say what the thing does for the reader.

voice.name: Pitch
voice.description: A peer with an opinion about what makes software hard, showing a reader who is deciding what tinyactors does about it, with proof under every claim.
voice.rule: The reader is "you"; contractions are fine. No "we": the product is the subject.
Open with a problem the reader has had, in their code or their words, before the answer: the tangle first, then the chart that removes it.
Name what makes the reader's software hard (logic spread across services, queues and callbacks with no owner) and say when distribution is worth its cost.
Each section is a few sentences and then the proof: code that ran, its output, or a claim with its source.
At most one concrete analogy per page, to something the reader runs ("like SQLite"); no decorative metaphors.
A comparison gives both sides real entries: what to choose tinyactors for, then what to choose the other for, each a verdict and one line of reason.

voice.name: How-to
voice.description: A colleague's runbook: the situation the reader is in, the steps that get them out, and what each line of code does.
voice.rule: The reader is "you"; contractions are fine. No "we".
Each section opens with the situation it solves, in the reader's terms, before the mechanism: "Most actors are waiting" before hibernation.
Under a block of code, one line for each part that matters, joining it to its effect ("…, so the room has one order without locks").
Carry one example, one order or one chat, through every section of a guide.
After an example, say in plain instructions what a production version adds: a store, a limit, an error path.

voice.name: Tutorial
voice.description: Someone at the learner's side: each step says what to do, what they will see and why it matters for what they are building.
voice.rule: The reader is "you"; contractions are fine. No "we".
A step's prose is passages of two or three sentences, up to 32 words each, varying in length; a one-line instruction stays a short paragraph.
A step opens with the problem the previous step left, says what you do, then shows the command or code and its output.
After the output, one sentence names what to look for in it and the one surprise it shows; no fact the step's own output does not show.
One thing is built across all the steps, and each step adds one idea to it.

voice.name: Explanation
voice.description: A chapter of a book that argues: a reader follows it from start to end to understand a design, and its costs, before depending on it.
voice.rule: The reader is "you"; "we" is the maintainers, for what they decided, measured or got wrong. Contractions are fine.
The lede sets the context a newcomer lacks: what the thing is, what problem the page explains, and what the reader can judge after it.
The prose is passages of up to five sentences, each at most 32 words, varying in length.
Each section opens with a problem, the concrete situation it solves with its stakes, never a question; passages build the idea, then a figure, a table or a claim with its source proves it.
Tell how the reader's system got where it is as a sequence of reasonable steps, then what it costs; say what the design does not fix.
Terms are introduced before they are used, and each section ends where the next one's question starts.
